A new study by cybersecurity firm Kaspersky, in collaboration with research consultancy VDC Strategy, estimated that the global average financial impact of a disruptive ransomware attack could exceed $470,000 per affected company.
The report, which assessed businesses across manufacturing, retail, healthcare, financial services and professional services, warned that the financial consequences extend beyond ransom payments to include business downtime, lost revenue, information technology recovery, incident response and legal expenses.
Europe recorded the highest estimated financial impact at $669,985 per company, followed by the Middle East with $486,497, Asia-Pacific at $439,292, Latin America at $432,321 and the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) at $425,969.
According to the study, ransom payments could account for approximately 49 per cent of the total financial impact, while the remaining costs arise from business interruption, recovery operations and other expenses required to restore affected systems.
The findings highlight the growing economic risks facing companies as they increasingly depend on digital platforms, cloud infrastructure, electronic payment systems and interconnected business applications.
Kaspersky’s threat statistics further showed that its security solutions detected 4,470 new ransomware modifications in the third quarter of 2026, representing an increase of approximately 76 per cent from the 2,538 recorded in the second quarter.
More than 81,000 users globally encountered ransomware attacks during the third quarter, compared with over 71,000 in the preceding quarter and more than 77,000 in the first quarter.
Commenting on the findings, Lead Security Researcher at Kaspersky’s Global Research and Analysis Team, Fabio Assolini, said organisations must look beyond ransom demands when assessing the financial implications of cyberattacks.
He said businesses needed to consider the wider costs of operational downtime, recovery and the resources required to restore their systems, adding that proactive protection, effective threat detection and adequate incident-response strategies were essential to reducing exposure.
Similarly, Director, Industrial Automation and Sensors at VDC Strategy, Jared Weiner, said putting a financial value on ransomware incidents would help business executives and security professionals understand the risks and make informed investment decisions.
The findings are particularly significant for Nigeria, where businesses are accelerating digital transformation across banking, telecommunications, retail, healthcare and public services.
A separate cybersecurity assessment by Check Point in February 2026 indicated that Nigerian organisations faced an average of 4,701 cyberattacks weekly, placing the country among Africa’s most targeted markets.
For businesses operating in Nigeria, a successful ransomware attack could disrupt payment processing, customer transactions, supply chains and access to critical business records, with consequences for revenue, consumer confidence and service delivery.
The Nigerian Data Protection Act 2023, enforced by the Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC), also places obligations on organisations to safeguard personal information and maintain appropriate data protection measures.
Consequently, companies facing cyber incidents may have additional regulatory and legal obligations, depending on the nature of the breach and the information affected. To reduce the risks, Kaspersky advised organisations to regularly update software, strengthen endpoint protection, monitor suspicious network activities and maintain offline data backups that cannot be accessed or altered by attackers.
It also recommended improved threat intelligence, professional cybersecurity training and effective incident-response arrangements to enable companies to detect attacks early and restore operations quickly.
The study further noted that its financial estimates did not include regulatory fines, litigation awards, long-term reputational damage or potential loss of customer trust, suggesting that the actual economic consequences could be higher.
